questions.q: State the domain of \((f+g)\) if \(f(x) = \sqrt{x-2}\) and \(g(x) = \frac{1}{x-3}\).
questions.a: The domain of \(f\) is \([2, \infty)\) and the domain of \(g\) is \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{3\}\). The domain of \(f+g\) is the intersection: \([2, \infty) \cap (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{3\}) = [2, 3) \cup (3, \infty)\). A wrong answer like \([2, \infty)\) reveals the student forgot to exclude \(x=3\) where \(g\) is undefined, or forgot that domain of sum is intersection, not union.

questions.q: Explain why the domain of \(\frac{f}{g}\) is not simply the intersection of domains of \(f\) and \(g\). Give an example where the domain of \(\frac{f}{g}\) is strictly smaller than \(\text{dom}(f) \cap \text{dom}(g)\).
questions.a: The domain of \(\frac{f}{g}\) must also exclude points where \(g(x)=0\) because division by zero is undefined. For example, let \(f(x)=x\) and \(g(x)=x-2\). Then \(\text{dom}(f)=\mathbb{R}\), \(\text{dom}(g)=\mathbb{R}\), intersection is \(\mathbb{R}\). But \(\frac{f}{g}(x)=\frac{x}{x-2}\) is undefined at \(x=2\), so its domain is \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{2\}\). A wrong answer indicates the student treats division like multiplication, ignoring the denominator-zero restriction.

questions.q: If \(f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1\) and \(g(x) = x - 4\), find \((fg)(x)\) and evaluate \((fg)(2)\).
questions.a: \((fg)(x) = (2x^2 - 3x + 1)(x - 4) = 2x^3 - 8x^2 - 3x^2 + 12x + x - 4 = 2x^3 - 11x^2 + 13x - 4\). Then \((fg)(2) = 2(8) - 11(4) + 13(2) - 4 = 16 - 44 + 26 - 4 = -6\). A wrong answer like \(-10\) suggests an error in polynomial multiplication (e.g., missing a term) or arithmetic mistake in evaluation.

questions.q: Two functions \(f\) and \(g\) have domains \(\text{dom}(f) = [-1, 5]\) and \(\text{dom}(g) = [0, 6]\). The function \(h = f - g\) is defined. If \(h(x) = 0\) has a solution at \(x = 5.5\), is this possible? Justify.
questions.a: No, it is not possible. The domain of \(h = f - g\) is \(\text{dom}(f) \cap \text{dom}(g) = [0, 5]\). The value \(x = 5.5\) is not in this intersection, so \(h(5.5)\) is undefined. A wrong answer (e.g., "yes") reveals the student thinks the domain of difference is the union or doesn't check domain intersection before solving equations.

questions.q: A student claims that for any two real functions \(f\) and \(g\), \((f+g)(x) = (g+f)(x)\) and \((f-g)(x) = (g-f)(x)\). Evaluate this claim and correct any false statement.
questions.a: The first statement is true: addition of functions is commutative because \((f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)=g(x)+f(x)=(g+f)(x)\). The second statement is false: subtraction is not commutative; \((f-g)(x)=f(x)-g(x) = -(g(x)-f(x)) = -(g-f)(x)\). A student who says both are true does not understand that subtraction of real numbers (and hence functions) is not commutative.

questions.q: Construct two different real functions \(f\) and \(g\) such that \((fg)(x) = x^2 - 9\) and \(\text{dom}(f) \cap \text{dom}(g) = \mathbb{R}\). State your functions and verify.
questions.a: Example: \(f(x) = x+3\), \(g(x) = x-3\). Then \((fg)(x) = (x+3)(x-3) = x^2 - 9\). Both domains are \(\mathbb{R}\), intersection is \(\mathbb{R}\). Another valid pair: \(f(x)=x^2-9\), \(g(x)=1\). A poor answer might give \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+3}\), \(g(x)=\sqrt{x-3}\) which have restricted domains, or might not verify the product.
